Introduction

Review the Submission section first so you know what you have to create and submit.

There are two levels of host systems that drive these devices. The first layer is the PCI layer, and the second is the VirtIO layer. Each of these devices is a virtual device using the VirtIO protocol. This is why we drove the UART and RTC in the last lab, and we will drive all of the VirtIO devices in this lab.

The initialization of each device will be done in handoff. The handoff starts with PCI to VirtIO and then VirtIO to the underlying device.

Finally, you will log all of the devices under the global kernel data device registry. Since you have a heap, you can use the alloc library.

Peripheral Component Interconnect (PCI)

Your main device bus is PCI, which has a comprehensive configuration and access mechanism called the "enhanced configuration access mechanism" or ECAM. It was enhanced for PCI express.

PCI-X is PCI "extended" and is not PCI express. PCI express is shortened to PCIe. PCI-X is just an enhancement over the original PCI using the same basic parallel architecture. PCI express is a serial, point-to-point architecture.

The starting point is to find the ECAM, which comes from ACPI from the MCFG table. This tells you the ECAM physical address as well as the starting and ending bus numbers. These will be important when we loop through the busses to find devices we can drive.

PCI Address Structure

The PCI physical memory addresses are broken down as follows.

Address Configuration Space

A[(20+n-1):20]

Bus number (n = \$\log_{2}(\text{end_bus_number}+1)=\[1..8]\$)

A[19:15]

Device number

A[14:12]

Function number

A[11:8]

Extended register number

A[7:2]

Register number

A[1:0]

Byte enables
The bus numbers are given to you in the MCFG ACPI table. Do not exceed the end bus number. Recall that it is inclusive in the MCFG table.

The PCI ECAM address can be a 32-bit or 64-bit address. Only the lower 28 bits contribute to the bus, device, function, and register numbers. The upper bits locate the ECAM MMIO space.

Example of 0x3076b000
31 28 27      20  19   15 14     12  11         8  7       2 1 0
0011  [00000111]  [01101] [  011  ]  [   0000   ]  [0000 00] 0 0
      [ Bus #  ]  [Dev #] [Func # ]  [Ext Reg # ]  [ Reg # ]

As you can see above, each device has \$2^{16}\$ = 65,536 bytes of space in ECAM, and each bus has \$2^{20}\$ = 1,048,576 bytes (1 MiB).

Calculating ECAM Offset
/// Calculate the ECAM offset given a bus and slot number
const fn ecam_offset(bus: u8, slot: u8) -> usize {
    let bus = bus as usize;
    let slot = slot as usize;
    debug_assert!((slot >> 5) == 0, "Slot (device) is more than 5 bits");
    // We don't need to assert bus since it's 8 bits to start with.
    (bus << 20) | (slot << 15)
}

ECAM Structure (PCI § 6.1)

The ECAM device index is encoded in the MMIO address with the bus and slot encoded to find the top of the ECAM for that device.

There are three things you are looking for at the very beginning. First, look for the vendorid. If this is 0xFFFF, then it is telling you that there is nothing connected here. Otherwise, a VirtIO device will have a vendor id of 0x1AF4. The device id will be the particular VirtIO device. Device IDs are encoded starting with 0x1040 plus the virtIO device number.

You are looking at the header_type. A type 0 header is a device whereas type 1 is a bridge. Luckily, EDK2 has already setup all of the bridges for us, so we only care about type 0 devices.

ECAM Header

You can see above the "Header Type" field, which is either 0 (device) or 1 (bridge) as well as the 16-bit Device ID and Vendor ID fields.

ECAM in Rust

Rust does not like unions (even though it still has them) as well as structures without a specific size. We will write methods to locate data instead and do type conversions. We will see that we will need to do this again in VirtIO.

Just like a lot of the ACPI tables, we can wrap the ECAM in a structure. The first thing we need to check is the header type, since type 0 has different fields than type 1. However, both types are the same size since the ECAM address is packed with the bus, slot, and register numbers.

The first 16 bytes of the ECAM gives us all of the information we need for: (1) determining whether a device is actually connected (check vendorid == 0xFFFF) and (2) the layout of the rest of the structure (based on header_type).

/// The first section of ECAM that is common for both type-0 and type-1 PCI devices.
#[repr(C)]
pub struct CommonEcam {
    pub vendor_id: u16,
    pub device_id: u16,
    pub command_reg: u16,
    pub status_reg: u16,
    pub revision_id: u8,
    pub class_code: [u8; 3],
    pub cache_line_size: u8,
    pub latency_timer: u8,
    pub header_type: PciType,
    pub bist: u8,  // built-in self test
}
impl CommonEcam {
    /// Wrap a PCI ECAM base (from ACPI) at the given bus and slot
    pub fn new(base: VirtualAddress, bus: u8, slot: u8) -> &'static mut Self {
        let bus = bus as usize;
        let slot = slot as usize;
        let ptr = base.add(ecam_offset(bus, slot)).as_mut_ptr();
        unsafe {
            ptr.as_mut_unchecked()
        }
    }
    /// Get the PCI type (bridge or device)
    pub fn get_type(&self) -> PciType {
        self.header_type
    }
}
#[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone, Eq, PartialEq, Ord, PartialOrd)]
#[repr(u8)]
pub enum PciType {
    Device = 0,
    Bridge = 1,

Capabilities (PCI § 6.7)

Capabilities are device-specific, but they are written in PCI ECAM space. This is a linked list with a capability ID and a next pointer. Also, the capability ID determines the size of the capability.

A device only has capabilities if bit index 4 of the status register is 1. Otherwise, there are no capabilities, and reading these fields is an error. Recall that the status register (bits [6:7]) is in the ECAM header for the particular device as well as the command register (bits [4:5]).

/// # The first 2 bytes of a capability.
///
/// Capabilities may expand the size, but the first two fields
/// are always id and next, respectively.
#[repr(C)]
pub struct Capability {
    pub id: u8,      // Capability identifier
    pub next: u8,    // Byte offset to the next capability
}

The capabilities are where we will find the configuration space for the virtual IO devices. The id gives you the structure of the capability itself, the Capability structure above is just the common first two fields of all capabilities. The next field is a byte offset from the start of the capability list to find the next capability. It is not a memory pointer (it’s only 8 bits), but you can think of it as a next pointer in a linked list. The capabilities are not necessarily in ascending order, so you have to be able to walk the capability list to find all capabilities.

MSI-X Capability (PCI § 6.8.2)

When configuring message signaled interrupts, we have to turn off the legacy interrupt, which is bit index 3 in the command register. If this is set to 1, it will interrupt the normal way, otherwise, if it is set to 0, it expects MSI/MSI-X to signal interrupts.

The MSI-X capability’s ID is 0x11 whereas the older MSI is 0x05.
All responses from your PCI devices will be signaled using MSI-X.

MSI-X Initial State (PCI § 6.8.2.3)

MSI-X is initially disabled at boot time, and you will be required to enable it by: (1) disabling interrupts via the command register for this particular device and (2) enabling MSI-X by setting bit index 15 of the message control register.

Virtual IO (virtio)

VirtIO devices are paravirtualized devices. Since paravirtualized devices know they are virtual, they are easier to configure, and they are more efficient to drive. All virtio devices have the same request/response system, but there are subtle differences between the bus. Since all of our virtio devices will be connected via PCI, we will use the PCI bus for discovery and configuration.

VirtIO Capabilities (Virtio § 4.1.4)

If the capability id is 0x09, then this is a vendor specific capability. There are five defined vendor specific capabilities for VirtIO. When you know you have a virtio device (vendorid = 0x1AF4) and a vendor-specific capability (id = 0x09), then the capability will take the following structure (including the id and next pointer).

/// # Calculate the offset in the BAR to find the given notification register
///
/// ## Arguments
///
/// . `offset` - the BAR offset from the `VirtioPciCapablity` structure.
/// . `queue_notify_offset` - comes from `queue_notify_offset` from `cfg_type = 1` structure.
/// . `notify_multiplier` - comes from `cfg_type = 2` structure.
pub const bar_notify(offset: u32, queue_notify_offset: u32, notify_multiplier: u32) -> usize {
    let o = offset as usize;
    let qno = queue_notify_offset as usize;
    let nm = notify_multiplier as usize;
    // Offset is the starting point, then we multiply the queue notify offset by the
    // capability multiplier.
    o + qno * nm
}

We can now take the BAR address in the bar field in the VirtioPciCapability and then add bar_notify to it.

If it did, we can read bit index 0 in the queue_irq field to see if it’s a queue interrupting. If bit index 1 is set, then it is telling you that it is interrupting because the device’s configuration has changed. The upper 30 bits are reserved and not used.

Device Specific (cfg_type = 4)

Each device ID has a different device-specific structure, and this is how we control the specific device itself.

PCI Configuration (cfg_type = 5)

We won’t need this configuration type because we can get everything we need from the device itself. This is just a mirror of the PCI configuration space (ECAM).

Virtual Queues (virtqueues) (Virtio § 2.6)

A virtual queue is memory used to make device requests and receive device responses. The size of the queue can be configured in software, and the queue size controls the three areas of a virtqueue.

All memory addresses are physical since we are not using an IOMMU.

A virtqueue has three parts: (1) descriptor table (array), (2) driver ring, and (3) device ring. A descriptor is a fundamental structure for making a request. The driver ring is where we place the descriptor index to make requests of a virtio devices. The device ring is where a device places its response.

Alignment

Size

\$6 + 2\times\text{Queue Size}\$

The VirtIO specification has two names for the rings. The driver ring is also called the "available" ring, and the device ring is also called the "used" ring for available buffers and used buffers, respectively.

  1. Each descriptor is exactly 16 bytes, and the array has queue size number of them, thus 16 * queue_size is the total number of bytes for the descriptor table.

  2. The driver ring has three fields and the ring. The three fields are all 2 bytes (u16). Then, the driver ring has two-byte elements, which are u16, and there are queue size number of them.

  3. The device ring has three fields and the ring. The three fields are all 2 bytes (u16). Then, the device ring has a structure with 8 bytes (DeviceUsedElement) for each element, and there are queue size number of them.

Rust does not like run-time sized data, so you will need to use methods to locate the data rather than the structure itself. You will notice that I put the field down, but I comment it out so we can locate it.

For PCI devices, the queue size is configured in the PCI common configuration capability structure (config type 1).

The index field is a wrapping value from 0 - 65535. When we increase the index, it is "seen" by the device, and it can look at its index % queue size to read the 16-bit value. This 16-bit value is an index into the descriptor table. The device then reads that descriptor and performs its action. What the descriptor is describing depends on the device. For example, for the entropy device, the descriptor is a set of bytes in memory that the entropy device will write into, and for the block device, the address points to a block header which describes where to read or write data, the direction (read vs. write), where in memory to read or write to, and how much (length).

Descriptor Flags

The descriptor’s third field is the flags field. This can be 0 (no flags).

The Write flag sets a direction for the DMA request. If you specify Write, the device is WRITE-ONLY. This is important to keep in mind since it seems like it just gives the device permission to write. However, a device read will fail if Write is set.

Handoff

The individual devices go through several subsystems prior to being initialized. Each device has to be specifically initialized, since initializing a GPU is not the same as initializing a block device.

To get to the device:

  1. Go through pci_init.

  2. Handoff all pci.vendorid == 0x1AF4 to virtio_pci_init.

    1. From here, descriptor table and both rings are created in memory.

  3. Handoff all virtio devices to the device driver to drive.

    1. Entropy

    2. Block

    3. Input

    4. GPU

The block driver and GPU driver will be the most involved as there are a lot of initialization and packets to send to the block device.

VirtIO Initialization

All virtio devices are initialized as follows.

  1. Reset the device by writing 0 in the device_status field.

  2. Set the ACKNOWLEDGE status bit (bit index 0). This tells the device you noticed it.

  3. Set the DRIVER status bit (bit index 1) if it’s a device you can drive.

  4. Read the device feature bits and write the subset of feature bits understood by the OS and driver to the device.

    1. During this step, the driver MAY read (but MUST NOT write) the device-specific configuration fields to check that it can support the device before accepting it.

  5. Set the FEATURES_OK status bit (bit index 3). The driver MUST NOT accept new feature bits after this step.

  6. Re-read the device status to ensure the FEATURES_OK bit is still set.

    1. If it is not, the device does not support the features we requested.

  7. Perform device-specific setup, including discovery, setting the virtqueues.

  8. After everything is done, set the device live by writing DRIVER_OK status bit (bit index 2).

The bits are not in order. You write 1, then 2, then 8, then finally 4. I don’t know why, but we just have to deal with it NOT being 1, 2, 4, 8.

Entropy Device

This is the easiest device to test, which is why it is our first device. There isn’t much device-specific initialization. After you’ve created the descriptor table, driver ring, and device ring, you can start making requests.

To make an entropy request:

  1. Allocate the next descriptor in the descriptor table.

  2. Set the address to the physical address of the buffer you want to store a random value.

    1. You should use mmu_translate to convert the virtual address into a physical address.

  3. Set the size to the number of bytes you want the RNG to write.

  4. Put the descriptor index into the driver ring.

    1. Recall that there are queue_size number of descriptors in the table.

    2. You will need to put the next index \$\mod\$ queue_size.

  5. Increment the driver ring’s index (it naturally wraps at \$2^{16}\$).

    1. Do NOT mod the driver ring index (idx). The device expects this to wrap.

  6. Notify the device by selecting the appropriate virtqueue and writing to the notify register.

The random number generator will place random bytes into the buffer. When it is finished producing all of the requested bytes, it will send an interrupt, which will be handled by the PLIC. The PLIC hands off all PCI interrupts to your PCI subsystem.

After, the device ring will have an updated index, in which you can get the id and length of the response. The id will correspond with the descriptor it is answering.

Block Device

The block device will be the most important for your next lab which will load processes and schedule them. You will be able to test the next lab without having a working block driver, but it will be important to get the block driver completed.

The block device has three separate portions of a packet, so each request required three descriptors: (1) the header, which contains the sector and size, (2) the data buffer to read (IN) or write (OUT), (3) a one byte status field.

There are many problems you can face that will trip you up here. For example, if you try to read without setting the data buffer flags to WRITE, the request will fail. By the same token, if you are writing data to the block device, you cannot have WRITE set on the second descriptor.
The WRITE flag is not a permission, it is a direction. Recall that if the WRITE flag is set, the device may ONLY write to that memory. Otherwise, it may ONLY read from that memory.

The same goes for if your header has a size field that is not a multiple of the sector size (512), the request will fail.

const SECTOR_SIZE: usize = 512;

/// Virtio Block Request Types
#[repr(u32)]
enum BlockRequestType {
    In = 0,             // Read
    Out = 1,            // Write
    Flush = 4,          // Flush
    GetId = 8,          // Get device ID string
    GetLifetime = 10,   // Get device lifetime
    Discard = 11,       // Trim command
    WriteZeroes = 13,   // Write all zeroes
    SecureErase = 14,   // Delete and write all zeroes
}

/// VirtIO Block Header
#[repr(C)]
struct BlockHeader {
    pub request_type: BlockRequestType,
    pub reserved: u32,
    pub sector: u64,    // byte_offset / SECTOR_SIZE (512)
}

We can then define the rest of the data. These will be chained using three descriptors: (1) header, (2) data, and (3) status.

The request_type field describes the direction where IN is a read and OUT is a write. This will be very important as above since you will also need to set the proper WRITE flag for a IN.

The sector field is the starting sector to read. A sector is 512 bytes, so if you can only read in multiples of 512 bytes. For example, if you want to start at byte 530, you have to read bytes 512 - 529 in sector 1 (\$\floor{530 \div 512} = 1\$).

Data Descriptor

The data descriptor points to the physical address of the memory buffer that will either send (write/OUT) data to the block device or receive (read/IN) data from the block device.

You must ensure you give a physical address to the memory buffer. We don’t have an IOMMU, so the devices have no idea what your virtual addresses mean.

The size of the data descriptor is the size of the request in bytes. The size must be a multiple of the sector size. You will get an unsupported status if it is not.

Example Buffer Size

If I want 778 bytes from sector 4, I need to align 778 up to the next multiple of 512: 1024. Since I’m requesting more than I need, I will need to keep track of the original request in the buffer. This is typically stored in the resource control block when we start writing processes. For this lab, it can just be a separate structure.

The buffer I send to the block device is not necessarily the same buffer used in the request. There are a couple of reasons for this: (1) the OS needs to make sure user space has appropriate access to the memory and (2) the buffer to the block device needs to be a multiple of the sector size (512).

Creating a Buffer

The buffer address will be sent as a physical address to the host. However, because we don’t have any allocator that guarantees physical continuity, we will always dole out one page (4,096 bytes) regardless of the size. If we want more data than 4,096 bytes, we would have to chain multiple requests.

You will need to store this information for every request so that we can copy the buffer into the final destination as well as free all resources once the request is complete.

Status Descriptor

The status descriptor is one byte that the device will write to (so ensure Write is set) to tell you the status of the request.

Since it is possible that the device will not write to the status field, I recommend setting the status field to a sentinel value, like 111 so that you can distinguish it from 0 (SUCCESS).

The status values have the following meanings.

Status Descriptor
#[repr(u8)]
enum ReportedStatus {
    Ok = 0,
    IoError = 1,
    Unsupported = 2,
    Sentinel = 111,
}
impl Default for ReportedStatus {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self::Sentinel
    }
}
#[repr(C)]
struct Status {
    pub status: ReportedStatus,
}

  1. The Ok response means that the request was successful. Notice that it is also the value 0, so be careful!

  2. The IoError response means that there was a problem with the device itself. Either the device was removed or had a hiccup during the request, or you requested a sector that doesn’t exist.

  3. The Unsupported response means that you made a request that the device cannot respond to.

  4. The Sentinel is not a response, but instead the initial value to ensure you got a response.

Make sure you set the status byte’s descriptor flags to Write since the device needs permission to write the status. Also, since this is the end of the descriptor chain, make sure the Next flag is cleared.

Request Cycle

After you setup the request, you should notify that specific queue to get the device to read.

  1. Fill out the header descriptor.

    1. The header is read only, so ensure WRITE is cleared.

    2. Set the .next field to the data descriptor index, so ensure NEXT is set.

  2. Fill out the data descriptor.

    1. Set WRITE if this is a read request.

    2. Clear WRITE if this is a write request.

  3. Fill out the status descriptor.

    1. The WRITE flag must be set.

  4. Set the header descriptor ONLY in the driver ring.

    1. Increment the index in the driver ring by 1.

      1. You may think this should increase by 3, but this isn’t the number of descriptors you’re using. Instead, it is the number of ring elements specified.

When you increment the index in the driver ring, the device is free to start reading and responding to a request. So, make sure everything is setup correctly prior to incrementing the index.

The response will be placed in the device ring, and then the device will send an interrupt.

You will know if the request was successful by reading the status byte. If it is 0, the request is successful, so you can assume that your buffer either contains the data you wanted (read) or wrote the data to the disk (write).

Multiple Virtqueues

The block device allows you to configure multiple virtqueues. This is for performance reasons, and each queue is identical, but the block device will use a round-robin fashion in reading/writing these queues. You can configure this feature by negotiating VIRTIO_BLK_F_MQ and reading the num_queues field in the VirtioPciCommonCfg structure.

You are not required to implement multiple queues in this lab. To turn off multiple queues, clear the VIRTIO_BLK_F_MQ when negotiating the device features.

You need to be fast about receiving buffers and sending them back to the device. Therefore, when the input device interrupts, you should copy the values into a local buffer. Usually, the strategy for the buffer is to throw away future events when the buffer is full.

You must have a size limit, otherwise, you could easily run out of memory!

/// # Draw a line from (x1,y1) to (x2,y2)
///
/// ## Arguments
///
/// `x1` the starting column of the line.
/// `y1` the starting row of the line.
/// `x2` the ending column of the line.
/// `y2` the ending row of the line.
/// `screen_width` the width of the drawing surface (for wrapping).
/// `framebuffer` the pixel array to draw the line
/// `color` the pixel color of the line
pub fn draw_line(
    x1: usize,
    y1: usize,
    x2: usize,
    y2: usize,
    screen_width: usize,
    framebuffer: &mut [Pixel],
    color: Pixel,
) {
    let mut start_x = x1 as isize;
    let end_x = x2 as isize;
    let mut start_y = y1 as isize;
    let end_y = y2 as isize;
    let dx = x2.abs_diff(x1) as isize;
    let dy = -(y2.abs_diff(y1) as isize);
    let mut sx = 1_isize;
    let mut sy = 1_isize;

    // See if we're drawing right-to-left or left-to-right
    if x1 >= x2 {
        sx = -1;
    }
    // See if we're drawing top-to-bottom or bottom-to-top
    if y1 >= y2 {
        sy = -1;
    }

    // Calculate the starting error in delta x + delta y
    let mut error = dx + dy;
    loop {
        // `start_x` and `start_y` will move as we put down a pixel
        let pixel_location = start_y as usize * screen_width + start_x as usize;
        // Error check to make sure we don't exceed the framebuffer
        if pixel_location >= framebuffer.len() {
            debugln!(
                "Pixel location {} exceeded framebuffer size {}.",
                pixel_location,
                framebuffer.len()
            );
            break;
        }
        // If we get here, we're good to go and the pixel location has been
        // determined.
        framebuffer[pixel_location] = color;
        let e2 = 2 * error;
        // See if the error exceeds the delta y, which means the error is
        // going to grow.
        if e2 >= dy {
            if start_x == end_x {
                break;
            }
            // Update the amount of error
            error += dy;
            // Move the column to the next.
            start_x += sx;
        }
        // See if the error is within the x delta.
        if e2 <= dx {
            if start_y == end_y {
                break;
            }
            // Update the amount of error
            error += dx;
            // Move the row to the next.
            start_y += sy;
        }
    }
}

    buffer: &mut [Pixel],
    rect: Rectangle,
    fill: Pixel,
) {
    let width = screen_width as usize;
    let height = screen_height as usize;
    let top = rect.y as usize;
    let bottom = (rect.y + rect.height) as usize;
    let bottom = if bottom > height { height } else { bottom };
    let left = rect.x as usize;
    let right = (rect.x + rect.width) as usize;
    let right = if right > width { width } else { right };

    for row in top..bottom {
        for col in left..right {
            let pixel_loc = row * width + col;
            buffer[pixel_loc] = fill;
        }
    }
}

use crate::TERMINAL_FONT;

const STRING_SCALE_WIDTH: usize = 5;
const STRING_SCALE_HEIGHT: usize = 5;

/// # Draw a single character to frame buffer
///
/// ## Arguments
///
/// * `c` the ASCII character value
/// * `row` the row (x-val) on which to draw the char
/// * `col` the col (y-val) on which to draw the char
/// * `screen_width` the full screen width (for wrapping)
/// * `framebuffer` the frame buffer on which to draw the character
/// * `fgcolor` the font color
/// * `bgcolor` the behind-the-font color
pub fn draw_char(
    c: u8,
    row: u32,
    col: u32,
    screen_width: u32,
    framebuffer: &mut [Pixel],
    fgcolor: Pixel,
    bgcolor: Pixel
) {

    // Find the initial position for this character.
    let pos = c as usize * 1 * 16;  // 1 byte per row x 16 rows per char
    // 16 rows per character
    let row = (row as usize) * 16 * STRING_SCALE_HEIGHT;
    // 8 cols per character
    let col = (col as usize) * 8 * STRING_SCALE_WIDTH;

    // Since we're indexing `framebuffer`, we need everything to be `usize`.
    let width = screen_width as usize;

    // This assumes the font is exactly 8x16
    for i in 0..16 {
        for j in 0..8 {
            let color = if 0 != TERMINAL_FONT[pos + i] & (1 << j) {
                fgcolor
            } else {
                bgcolor
            };
            for k in 0..STRING_SCALE_WIDTH {
                for l in 0..STRING_SCALE_HEIGHT {
                    let at = (row + i * STRING_SCALE_HEIGHT + l) * width +
                             (col + j * STRING_SCALE_WIDTH + k);
                    framebuffer[at] = color;
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

/// # Draw characters to frame buffer
///
/// ## Arguments
///
/// * `s` the string of characters to draw
/// * `start_row` the starting row to draw
/// * `start_col` the starting col to draw
/// * `screen_width` the width of the screen for wrapping the string
/// * `framebuffer` the framebuffer to draw text into
/// * `fgcolor` the color to draw the font
/// * `bgcolor` the color to draw behind the font
///
/// ## Returns
///
/// Returns the invalidated rectangle for the string, which is the
/// bounding box of the pixels drawn.
pub fn draw_str(
    s: &str,
    start_row: u32,
    start_col: u32,
    screen_width: u32,
    framebuffer: &mut [Pixel],
    fgcolor: Pixel,
    bgcolor: Pixel,
) -> Rectangle
{
    let mut r = start_row;
    let mut c = start_col;
    // `draw_char` requires u8's, so get the string as bytes.
    let s_bytes = s.as_bytes();
    for i in 0..s.len() {
        // Reuse `draw_char` to draw in the right place.
        draw_char(
            s_bytes[i],
            r,
            c,
            screen_width,
            framebuffer,
            fgcolor,
            bgcolor,
        );
        c += 1;
        if c >= screen_width {
            // Wrap back to the next row and leftmost column
            r += 1;
            // If we set the following to 0, it goes all the way to the
            // left of the screen. This makes it more square so the starting
            // column is the leftmost for all of the drawn text.
            c = start_col;
        }
    }

    // We only redraw the portion of the screen that we modified. This
    // mitigates large memory transfers.
    Rectangle::new(
        start_col * STRING_SCALE_WIDTH as u32 * 8,
        start_row * STRING_SCALE_HEIGHT as u32 * 16,
        s.len() as u32 * 8 * STRING_SCALE_WIDTH as u32,
        16 * STRING_SCALE_HEIGHT as u32,
    )
}

Invalidating Pixels

It is important that you DO NOT redraw the entire screen every time. Instead, you need to make sure to transfer only pixels that have changed. Some times, this cannot be helped, such as clearing the screen, but the more you transfer, the longer it will take to redraw the pixels.

Updating Pixels

The transfer rectangle is pretty weird. If you don’t set the offset and rectangle properly, then you might not understand what pixels will be redrawn.

The offset is where in memory the host needs to start copying bytes from us. The host then copies it starting with pixel (rect.x, rect.y). It copies row by row and copies the rect.width * sizeof(Pixel) for every row.

/// Offset is a byte offset based on the size of a Pixel
fn calculate_transfer_offset(top: u64, left: u64, width: u64) -> u64 {
    const SOFPIX: u64 = core::mem::size_of::<Pixel>() as u64;
    left * SOFPIX + top * width * SOFPIX
}
